implementation_notes: Python's import system already is the mediating instance: importlib.import_module(name) resolves a dotted module name through the finders on sys.path (source files, zipimport, namespace packages, installed distributions) and returns the module, while sys.modules keeps the binding cache - a second import of the same name returns the cached module without touching the disk. importlib.invalidate_caches() tells the finders to forget their internal caches so modules created or installed while the program runs become visible, and that is the re-resolution hook; attribute names inside a module are then resolved with getattr. What replaces the classic structure is the language's own name resolution, so an explicit lookup service is only needed for resources that are not Python objects (remote endpoints, devices, data).
pitfalls: getattr raises AttributeError for a missing binding, indistinguishable from an attribute bug; convert it to a domain lookup error at the boundary and validate dotted names against an allow-list before importing untrusted input.
importlib.reload re-executes a module but does not rebind objects other modules imported from it - the documented stale-reference trap; callers must re-read the attribute or import the module itself.
Mutating sys.modules by hand changes resolution process-wide for every thread; restrict it to tests and debug tooling.

variants.name: Installed entry points (importlib.metadata)
variants.implementation_notes: For plugin discovery across installed distributions, importlib.metadata is the lookup service: entry_points(group="myapp.renderers") returns the declared entry points, select() filters by name or group, and EntryPoint.load() resolves the (module:attribute) value to the object. The bindings are declared by each distribution in its packaging metadata rather than in code, so registering a plugin is a deployment action and the new binding appears on the next query. Each EntryPoint also exposes .module, .attr and .dist, which lets the application inspect a binding before loading it.
pitfalls: One distribution can install several entry points and one top-level package can belong to several distributions, so entry-point names are not 1:1 with imports; use packages_distributions() when the mapping matters.
entry_points() reads installed metadata, so a binding can exist on disk before the code is importable - the failure appears at load(), not at query time.
Loading an untrusted entry point executes third-party code at lookup time; restrict the group and validate names.
